title: A Rat the Size of a Buffalo? The Biggest Rodents That Ever Lived
description: Animal Secrets #22. This month scientists named Yakamys sirindhornae, a roughly 30 kg rodent that lived in Thailand 33-35 million years ago, known from just two teeth (Scientific Reports, Nov 2026). We count down five giant rodents, from a coconut-chewing rat that fell out of a tree to a beaver the size of a bear and a one-tonne guinea pig cousin that used its teeth like tusks. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: She thought it was a bone. It was a rat's tooth.

scenes.label: Around 30 kg
scenes.say: This month, scientists in Thailand named a giant rodent from that tooth. It weighed around 30 kilos. That's 66 pounds.
And here's the crazy part. That's not even close to the biggest rodent that ever lived.

scenes.label: Wait for #1
scenes.say: Stick around, because number one had teeth a foot long. And it probably wasn't using them to eat.
Okay, so think about the rodents you know. A mouse. A rat. A squirrel. Small, fast, easy to miss.

scenes.label: 35 to 66 kg
scenes.say: The biggest rodent alive today is the capybara. Most weigh 35 to 66 kilos. A big wild female in Brazil hit 91.
It's basically a giant, chill guinea pig that can hold its breath underwater for up to five minutes.

scenes.label: 5 giant rodents
scenes.say: So today, five giant rodents. Each one is bigger than the last. And the last one would make a capybara look like a hamster.
Quick question before we start. How big do you think the biggest rodent ever got? Guess now. Keep it in your head.

scenes.label: Vangunu giant rat
scenes.say: Number five. A rat so rare that scientists had only ever seen one. And it fell out of a tree.
In 2017, scientists described a brand new species from the Solomon Islands. The Vangunu giant rat.

scenes.label: Only one specimen
scenes.say: The only specimen they had came from a tree that loggers cut down. The rat fell out with it.

scenes.label: Up to 1.5 feet
scenes.say: This thing can be up to a foot and a half long. That's at least twice the size of a common rat.

scenes.label: Cracks coconuts?
scenes.say: And local people say it chews through coconuts with its teeth. Up in the trees. A rat big enough to hug, cracking coconuts.
For years, nobody could photograph a live one. So researchers set up camera traps in the forest.

scenes.label: Peanut butter: fail
scenes.say: First they tried peanut butter. Bad idea. It only attracted ordinary black rats.

scenes.label: 95 photos, 4 rats
scenes.say: Then they switched to sesame oil. And it worked. 95 photos of four giant rats, almost all around midnight.
It was the first new rodent described from the Solomon Islands in over 80 years. But here's the sad twist.

scenes.label: Critically endangered
scenes.say: It lives on just one island, and the government has approved logging in its last forest. It's critically endangered.

scenes.label: Brand-new species
scenes.say: Number four. The giant from this month's news. And it all started with one lucky look at a rock.

scenes.label: Thailand, 2004
scenes.say: Back in 2004, geologist Pannipa Tian was working at a coal mine in Krabi, in southern Thailand.
She spotted something big and dark in the rock. At first, she thought it was a bone.

scenes.label: A giant front tooth
scenes.say: It was a front tooth. A rodent's gnawing tooth, so big her supervisor called it a giant rat's tooth.

scenes.label: Just two teeth
scenes.say: The same day, someone else on the team found a big molar. Two teeth. That's the whole animal.
More than twenty years later, a team from Thailand, France and Canada finally named it. Yakamys sirindhornae.
The second part of the name honors Thailand's Princess Sirindhorn. Not bad for a rat.
It belonged to the ischyromyids, one of the earliest big groups of rodents. They've been extinct for millions of years.

scenes.label: 33-35 million years
scenes.say: It lived 33 to 35 million years ago. Around 30 kilos. Roughly beaver-sized, about half a large capybara.
Now, here's the honest part. With only two teeth, nobody knows what it looked like or exactly how it lived.

scenes.label: Capybara-like?
scenes.say: The teeth were buried in old lake mud, so it may have lived like a capybara. But the team says that alone doesn't prove it.
Thirty kilos sounds huge for a rat. But compared to what's coming next? It's a snack-sized warm-up.

scenes.label: Giant beaver
scenes.say: Number three. A beaver the size of a bear. And it broke the number one beaver rule.

scenes.label: 10 to 35 kg
scenes.say: A normal North American beaver weighs 10 to 35 kilos. And it builds dams by chewing down trees.

scenes.label: Up to 100 kg
scenes.say: The giant beaver, Castoroides, weighed up to around 100 kilos. Bulky body, short legs, roughly bear-sized.

scenes.label: Skinny tail
scenes.say: And its tail wasn't the classic flat paddle. It was long and skinny, more like a muskrat's tail.
Its fossils turn up from Florida all the way to Alaska and the Yukon. It was everywhere.
And for tens of thousands of years, giant beavers and normal beavers lived side by side.
So you'd think a beaver that big would flatten whole forests, right? That's what scientists assumed for ages.

scenes.label: 2019 bone study
scenes.say: But in 2019, a team studied chemical signals locked in its bones and teeth. And the answer surprised everyone.

scenes.label: No trees!
scenes.say: It didn't eat trees at all. It ate soft plants growing underwater in lakes and swamps.
One researcher put it simply. They found no evidence the giant beaver cut down trees or ate them for food.
No tree cutting means no dams and no lodges. The little beaver could build. The giant one couldn't.
So when the Ice Age ended and the climate got drier, its wetlands shrank. And it had nowhere to go.

scenes.label: Gone 10,000 years ago
scenes.say: It disappeared around 10,000 years ago. The small beaver, the builder, survived. Being big wasn't enough.

scenes.label: Phoberomys
scenes.say: Number two. A guinea pig cousin as big as a buffalo. Seriously.

scenes.label: Guinea pig: 1 kg
scenes.say: A pet guinea pig weighs about one kilo. Now hold that picture in your head.

scenes.label: Venezuela, 2000
scenes.say: In 2000, scientists dug up a skeleton near the town of Urumaco, in northwestern Venezuela. About 90 percent complete.
They nicknamed it Goya. It lived about 8 million years ago, along the banks of an ancient river.
It probably fed on rough plants, maybe grasses near salty river water, and foraged right on the riverbanks.

scenes.label: About 700 kg
scenes.say: It was about three meters long and 1.3 meters tall. Estimated weight? Around 700 kilos.
That's more than ten times the weight of a capybara. From the same family tree as your guinea pig.
Its closest living relative is the pakarana, a chunky rodent from South American forests.
One scientist said to imagine a weird guinea pig, but huge, with a long tail for balancing on its hind legs.

scenes.label: Record holder... for now
scenes.say: In 2003, it was crowned the biggest rodent that ever lived. Scientists were sure the record would stand.
Nobody knows why it died out. But here's the twist. A few years later, a single skull from Uruguay stole its crown.

scenes.label: Biggest rodent ever
scenes.say: Number one. Josephoartigasia. The biggest rodent ever found. And its teeth weren't really for eating.

scenes.label: One skull, Uruguay
scenes.say: In 2007, a skull was found in Uruguay. Just one skull, and it was missing its lower jaw.

scenes.label: Around 1,000 kg
scenes.say: It lived about 3 million years ago, and scientists estimate it weighed around 1,000 kilos. A full tonne.
That beats Goya by about 300 kilos. Remember your guess from the start? Was it even close?

scenes.label: Foot-long teeth
scenes.say: And in the front of that skull? Two huge gnawing teeth, around a foot long.

scenes.label: Bite like a tiger
scenes.say: In 2015, scientists rebuilt the missing jaw on a computer and simulated its bite. About 1,400 newtons. Similar to a tiger.

scenes.label: 3x stronger teeth
scenes.say: But here's what made no sense. Its front teeth were strong enough to handle almost three times that force.
Why build teeth way stronger than your own bite? That's like buying a truck to carry one apple.

scenes.label: Teeth as tusks
scenes.say: The answer: it probably used them like tools. Digging in the ground for food, or defending itself from predators.
The lead scientist said it was very similar to how a modern elephant uses its tusks. A rodent with tusks.
So a bite like a tiger, but it probably wasn't much of a predator. It just had teeth tough enough for heavy work.
So the biggest rodent ever wasn't a monster rat. It was a one-tonne guinea pig cousin with built-in shovels.
And we only found it from one skull. Just like Yakamys, from two teeth. So how many giants are still hiding in rocks?

scenes.label: Your pick?
scenes.say: Which one surprised you most? The coconut rat, the beaver that couldn't build, or the rodent with tusks? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: A Geologist Found a Tooth From a 30-Kilo Rat
short.description: A geologist in Thailand thought she'd found a bone. It was the tooth of Yakamys sirindhornae, a roughly 30 kg rodent from 33-35 million years ago, named this month in Scientific Reports. The full countdown of the 5 biggest rodents ever is on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: A geologist found this tooth and thought it was a bone. It belonged to a giant rodent.

scenes.label: Thailand, 2004
scenes.say: It was 2004, at a coal mine in southern Thailand. She spotted something big and dark in the rock.

scenes.label: A front tooth
scenes.say: Her supervisor took one look. Not a bone. A giant rat's tooth.

scenes.label: Around 30 kg
scenes.say: This month, scientists finally named it. Yakamys. It lived 33 to 35 million years ago and weighed around 30 kilos.

scenes.label: Just two teeth
scenes.say: That's beaver-sized, about half a big capybara. All from just two teeth. Wild, right?

scenes.label: 1 tonne?!
scenes.say: And it's not even close to the biggest rodent ever. That one weighed a tonne. Full story on the channel.
So next time you see a weird rock, look twice. Because a geologist found this tooth and thought it was a bone.
